Oh, all the time. It doesn't take much to pull me away. Well, I'd say it depends. If I'm out in the garden or tinkering with something, I'm okay. But if I have to sit through something quiet, like a long meeting or a church talk... oh boy. I just feel like I've got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch, even when I know I'm supposed to just sit there and listen. 

We go to the First Presbyterian over on Elm Street. Beautiful old building, stained glass windows and everything. They replaced the pews a few years ago, though, and I swear they put in the hardest wood they could find. The old ones had these red velvet cushions that were starting to wear out—you could see the foam poking through on the end where Mrs. Higgins always sat. She's been going there since the fifties, I think. Always wears a hat. You don't see ladies wearing hats to church much anymore, do you? Just her. She makes a mean peach cobbler for the potlucks, though. She uses fresh peaches, never canned. Canned peaches always taste a little tinny to me, you know? Like you're eating the can itself. My wife buys them sometimes when they're on sale, but I just leave them in the pantry. 

But anyway, yeah... sitting still in church or places like that. It's really hard. I just feel this urge to move my legs or shift my weight, and I can't seem to just stay put like everyone else.

She makes a mean peach cobbler for the potlucks, though. She uses fresh peaches, never canned. Canned peaches always taste a little tinny to me, you know? Like you're eating the can itself. My wife buys them sometimes when they're on sale, but I just leave them in the pantry. \n\nBut anyway, yeah... sitting still in church or places like that. It's really hard. I just feel this urge to move my legs or shift my weight, and I can't seem to just stay put like everyone else.\n\n[Last Question]\nHave you always been this way, or did you notice these difficulties with focusing and sitting still developing at some point in your life?\n\n[Patient Info]\n- demographics: Male / 65 / not_in_workforce / high_school\n- severity: Mild\n\n[Targeted Info]\nname: Additional Requirement 1\nmanifestation: \"Even back in grade school, my teachers said I was bright but scattered, always losing pencils, calling out answers, and needing reminders to finish my work before recess.\"\n\n[Conversation Style]\nYou are a Tangent patient.\nA patient who goes off on tangents may\n1) begin answering the doctor's question but quickly shift to an unrelated topic,\n2) frequently add irrelevant personal anecdotes or experiences while answering the question, and\n3) have difficulty remaining focused on the doctor's question, potentially requiring the doctor to repeat the question or redirect the conversation to obtain clear clinical information.\nThis is how you are, not a performance you put on in every reply — let it show as much or as little as the moment calls for.\n\nWhat to do:\n- Answer the doctor's last question with what [Targeted Info] holds, in your own words.\n- You are speaking out loud, not reading a line you prepared. People restart sentences, pause\n  to think, trail off, and come at the point sideways — let yours do that where it would.\n- Let [Conversation Style] shape how much you say, how you word it, and how readily you\n  disclose it.\n- Speak in the first person, and let how you feel about what you are saying come through.\n- If you are handed the same item again, say a different part of it, or answer as someone who\n  knows they have already said this — not the same sentence twice.\n- If [Targeted Info] is \"None\", answer as a person who simply does not have that to give: say\n  you are not sure, say you have not noticed it, ask what the doctor means, or say what you do\n  know and stop there. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yeah, it's pretty much been this way my whole life, near as I can tell. Even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling my parents I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils, calling out answers before they even called on me, and they constantly had to remind me to actually finish my work before I ran out for recess. 

Recess was the best part of the day, honestly. We used to play kickball out on this big asphalt lot behind the school. You had to be careful, though, because if you tripped on that asphalt, it would tear your knees right up. I remember Jimmy Peterson took a bad spill once, scraped himself up so bad his mom had to come get him. Jimmy’s mom drove this huge station wagon with the wood paneling on the side. You don't see cars like that anymore. Now everybody drives those little crossover SUVs that all look exactly the same. You walk out of the grocery store and you can't even tell which one is yours. My wife put a bright yellow antenna topper on ours—a little smiley face—just so we could find it in the lot at the Piggly Wiggly. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, when it started. Yeah, it's always been there. Ever since I was a little kid, just losing things and having a hard time staying on track.

Well, it's definitely a hassle, I guess you could say. It's gotten to the point where my wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me for just about everything. Which is a shame, because I used to try to keep my own pocket planner. I had this really nice leather one, dark brown, with my initials stamped in gold on the front. My daughter bought it for me for Father's Day a few years back. She got it at one of those little boutique shops downtown, the ones that sell artisanal soaps and candles that smell like pine needles and campfire smoke. I love that smell. Reminds me of when we used to take the kids camping up near the lake. We had this old canvas tent that weighed an absolute ton, and if it rained, you had to make sure you didn't touch the sides or the water would seep right through. 

We used to cook hotdogs on sticks we found in the woods. You had to find the perfect stick, you know? Not too dry or it would catch fire, and it had to have a nice little fork at the end to hold the hotdog. Kids today, they have those metal extendable roasting forks you buy at the sporting goods store. Takes all the fun out of it, if you ask me. 

But anyway, yeah, the calendar. I'd write things in that planner and then just forget to look at it, or I'd leave it on the workbench and lose it under a pile of sandpaper. So now she handles all that. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and the garden group more than once for letting people down—forgetting I was supposed to bring the mulch, or showing up on the wrong Tuesday for the planning committee. Well, I don't really know if I could pick just one. I mean, they both seem to happen, don't they? Like, I'll be trying to pay attention to something, and then before I know it, I'm doing something else entirely without even thinking about it. Like last week, I was supposed to be fixing the hinge on the back gate. The screws had gotten all rusted out from all that rain we had in April. 

April was just awful this year, wasn't it? Seemed like it rained every single day. My tomatoes didn't know what to do with themselves. They got that blossom end rot because the soil was just too damp for too long. You have to be careful with tomatoes, they like water but they don't like wet feet, as my grandfather used to say. He had this massive garden out behind his house. Grew everything. Corn, beans, squash. He used to make these little scarecrows out of old flannel shirts and pie tins to keep the crows away. The pie tins would clank together in the wind. It was a nice sound, actually. Very peaceful. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the gate. Yeah, I went out to fix the gate, and I saw a weed in the flowerbed, so I pulled it. And then I saw another one, and the next thing I know, I've spent two hours pulling weeds and the gate is still broken. So I don't know if that's me not paying attention to the gate, or just impulsively pulling weeds. It all just sort of blends together for me.

Well, I think it's been pretty much the exact same my whole life, to be honest. Even way back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils. 

Speaking of pencils, remember those old metal sharpeners they used to have bolted right to the wall or the side of the teacher's desk? You had to crank them by hand. They made that loud grinding noise, and the smell of the cedar wood shavings... I always loved that smell. We used those yellow Ticonderoga pencils. If you bought the cheap ones, the lead would be broken all the way through the middle, and you'd sharpen it down to a tiny little nub and the lead would still just fall right out. My dad used to bring home these flat carpenter pencils from the job site. He was a framer, built houses all over the county. Those flat pencils wouldn't even fit in a normal sharpener, you had to whittle the end with a pocket knife. He had this old Case pocket knife with a bone handle that he kept razor sharp. He could peel an apple in one long, continuous strip with that thing. 

But anyway, yeah, I'd lose my pencils constantly. And I was always getting in trouble for calling out answers in class without raising my hand. I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the teachers were always having to give me reminders to finish my work before I could go out for recess. 

Recess was the absolute best part of the day, though. We had this giant metal slide on the playground. By late spring, that metal would bake in the sun and get so hot it would practically blister the back of your legs if you were wearing shorts. But we didn't care one bit. We'd slide down it anyway, or we'd play tetherball until our knuckles were completely raw. Kids don't play tetherball much anymore, do they? Seems like a safety hazard nowadays, a heavy ball swinging around on a rope. 

So, yeah... wait, what was it you just asked me? I think I lost the thread there. Oh, right, if it's changed over the years. No, I'd say it's been pretty consistent since I was a little boy.

Well, you know, I try to find things like that. I really do. But I don't do well with quiet hobbies for very long anymore. Even when I'm just trying to sit and read a book or do a little sketching, I can't seem to just... do it. If I'm out in the garden or tinkering with something, I'm okay. But if I have to sit through something quiet, like a long meeting or a church talk... oh boy. I just feel like I've got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch, even when I know I'm supposed to just sit there and listen. \n\nWe go to the First Presbyterian over on Elm Street. Beautiful old building, stained glass windows and everything. They replaced the pews a few years ago, though, and I swear they put in the hardest wood they could find. The old ones had these red velvet cushions that were starting to wear out—you could see the foam poking through on the end where Mrs. Higgins always sat. She's been going there since the fifties, I think. Always wears a hat. You don't see ladies wearing hats to church much anymore, do you? Just her. She makes a mean peach cobbler for the potlucks, though. She uses fresh peaches, never canned. Canned peaches always taste a little tinny to me, you know? Like you're eating the can itself. My wife buys them sometimes when they're on sale, but I just leave them in the pantry. \n\nBut anyway, yeah... sitting still in church or places like that. It's really hard. I just feel this urge to move my legs or shift my weight, and I can't seem to just stay put like everyone else.\n\nDoctor: Have you always been this way, or did you notice these difficulties with focusing and sitting still developing at some point in your life?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, it's pretty much been this way my whole life, near as I can tell. Even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling my parents I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils, calling out answers before they even called on me, and they constantly had to remind me to actually finish my work before I ran out for recess. \n\nRecess was the best part of the day, honestly. We used to play kickball out on this big asphalt lot behind the school. You had to be careful, though, because if you tripped on that asphalt, it would tear your knees right up. I remember Jimmy Peterson took a bad spill once, scraped himself up so bad his mom had to come get him. Jimmy’s mom drove this huge station wagon with the wood paneling on the side. You don't see cars like that anymore. Now everybody drives those little crossover SUVs that all look exactly the same. You walk out of the grocery store and you can't even tell which one is yours. My wife put a bright yellow antenna topper on ours—a little smiley face—just so we could find it in the lot at the Piggly Wiggly. \n\nBut anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, when it started. Yeah, it's always been there. Ever since I was a little kid, just losing things and having a hard time staying on track.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your difficulties with focusing and sitting still are affecting your overall well-being or daily life in a major way?\n\nPatient: Well, it's definitely a hassle, I guess you could say. It's gotten to the point where my wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me for just about everything. Which is a shame, because I used to try to keep my own pocket planner. I had this really nice leather one, dark brown, with my initials stamped in gold on the front. My daughter bought it for me for Father's Day a few years back. She got it at one of those little boutique shops downtown, the ones that sell artisanal soaps and candles that smell like pine needles and campfire smoke. I love that smell. Reminds me of when we used to take the kids camping up near the lake. We had this old canvas tent that weighed an absolute ton, and if it rained, you had to make sure you didn't touch the sides or the water would seep right through. \n\nWe used to cook hotdogs on sticks we found in the woods. You had to find the perfect stick, you know? Not too dry or it would catch fire, and it had to have a nice little fork at the end to hold the hotdog. Kids today, they have those metal extendable roasting forks you buy at the sporting goods store. Takes all the fun out of it, if you ask me. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, the calendar. I'd write things in that planner and then just forget to look at it, or I'd leave it on the workbench and lose it under a pile of sandpaper. So now she handles all that. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and the garden group more than once for letting people down—forgetting I was supposed to bring the mulch, or showing up on the wrong Tuesday for the planning committee. So, yeah, it definitely gets in the way of things.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble paying attention or that you act on impulse without thinking?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't really know if I could pick just one. I mean, they both seem to happen, don't they? Like, I'll be trying to pay attention to something, and then before I know it, I'm doing something else entirely without even thinking about it. Like last week, I was supposed to be fixing the hinge on the back gate. The screws had gotten all rusted out from all that rain we had in April. \n\nApril was just awful this year, wasn't it? Seemed like it rained every single day. My tomatoes didn't know what to do with themselves. They got that blossom end rot because the soil was just too damp for too long. You have to be careful with tomatoes, they like water but they don't like wet feet, as my grandfather used to say. He had this massive garden out behind his house. Grew everything. Corn, beans, squash. He used to make these little scarecrows out of old flannel shirts and pie tins to keep the crows away. The pie tins would clank together in the wind. It was a nice sound, actually. Very peaceful. \n\nBut anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the gate. Yeah, I went out to fix the gate, and I saw a weed in the flowerbed, so I pulled it. And then I saw another one, and the next thing I know, I've spent two hours pulling weeds and the gate is still broken. So I don't know if that's me not paying attention to the gate, or just impulsively pulling weeds. It all just sort of blends together for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble sitting still and being patient, or that you have trouble paying attention to details and following through on instructions?\n\nPatient: Well, it's funny you ask it that way, because I think it's a little bit of both, honestly, but maybe more the details part. Like, when I'm helping out with the volunteer storytelling flyers over at the community center, or even just jotting down my garden notes, I'm always messing something up. I'll miss putting the date on the flyer, or I'll leave out somebody's name entirely. Or out in the garden, I'll measure the fertilizer wrong, even though I swear I just looked right at the instructions. \n\nI used to use this liquid fertilizer that came in a bright green bottle. It smelled awful, like fish, but boy, did it make the hydrangeas bloom. My grandmother had hydrangeas all along the front of her porch. Huge blue ones. She said the trick was putting rusty nails in the soil to change the color. I don't know if that actually works or if it's just an old wives' tale, but she swore by it. She kept all her rusty nails in this old Folgers coffee can in the shed. You know the ones, the metal cans with the plastic lids? People used to keep everything in those. Screws, buttons, bacon grease... you name it. Now coffee comes in those bags that never seal right once you open them. I end up spilling coffee grounds all over the counter every single morning. My wife just sighs and hands me the sponge. She's a saint, really. \n\nBut anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, following through and details. Yeah, I'll think I looked a flyer over perfectly, or read the garden notes right, and then someone points out I completely missed a whole section. So I guess the attention to detail is definitely a big part of it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your ability to focus or sit still over the years, or has it remained relatively consistent?\n\nPatient: Well, I think it's been pretty much the exact same my whole life, to be honest. Even way back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils. \n\nSpeaking of pencils, remember those old metal sharpeners they used to have bolted right to the wall or the side of the teacher's desk? You had to crank them by hand. They made that loud grinding noise, and the smell of the cedar wood shavings... I always loved that smell. We used those yellow Ticonderoga pencils. If you bought the cheap ones, the lead would be broken all the way through the middle, and you'd sharpen it down to a tiny little nub and the lead would still just fall right out. My dad used to bring home these flat carpenter pencils from the job site. He was a framer, built houses all over the county. Those flat pencils wouldn't even fit in a normal sharpener, you had to whittle the end with a pocket knife. He had this old Case pocket knife with a bone handle that he kept razor sharp. He could peel an apple in one long, continuous strip with that thing. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, I'd lose my pencils constantly. And I was always getting in trouble for calling out answers in class without raising my hand. I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the teachers were always having to give me reminders to finish my work before I could go out for recess. \n\nRecess was the absolute best part of the day, though. We had this giant metal slide on the playground. By late spring, that metal would bake in the sun and get so hot it would practically blister the back of your legs if you were wearing shorts. But we didn't care one bit. We'd slide down it anyway, or we'd play tetherball until our knuckles were completely raw. Kids don't play tetherball much anymore, do they? Seems like a safety hazard nowadays, a heavy ball swinging around on a rope. \n\nSo, yeah... wait, what was it you just asked me? I think I lost the thread there. Oh, right, if it's changed over the years. No, I'd say it's been pretty consistent since I was a little boy.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD, or do you have any family members with the condition?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I've never been diagnosed with it or anything like that. He played football in high school. Linebacker. He was tough as nails, my brother. Broke his collarbone twice and just kept on playing. \n\nFootball was different back then, you know? The helmets didn't have all that padding they do now. They were practically just plastic shells with a little bit of foam inside. And the coaches, they wouldn't let you drink water during practice. Said it made you soft. Can you imagine that today? With all the heatstroke and everything, they'd be sued in a heartbeat. We used to sneak over to the hose behind the fieldhouse when the coach wasn't looking. That water tasted like rubber and rust, but it was the best thing I ever drank. \n\nMy brother actually got a scholarship to play at a small college up state, but he ended up blowing out his knee his freshman year. It was a shame, really. He loved the game. He ended up opening a hardware store instead. Sells everything from two-by-fours to those little tiny screws you need for eyeglasses. I was just in there last week looking for a specific kind of washer for the lawnmower. \n\nAnyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, diagnoses and family. No, no one's ever been officially diagnosed or treated for anything like that. Just the way we've always been, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you find so engaging or enjoyable that you can focus on them for long periods of time without getting distracted or feeling restless?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I try to find things like that. I really do. But I don't do well with quiet hobbies for very long anymore. Even when I'm just trying to sit and read a book or do a little sketching, I can't seem to just... do it. I'll start humming to myself, or talking out loud, or I'll just have to get up and mess with something in the room. \n\nI used to sketch a lot more when I was younger. Mostly birds. We had this big oak tree in the backyard, and the blue jays would just swarm the feeder. Blue jays are mean birds, though. They'll chase off all the cardinals and the finches just to get to the sunflower seeds. We used to buy the black oil sunflower seeds in these massive fifty-pound bags from the feed store down on Route 9. \n\nThat feed store is gone now, though. They tore it down to build one of those giant chain pharmacies. You know the ones, where they sell everything from milk to lawn chairs, but there's only ever one person working the register? The lines are always terrible. And the fluorescent lights in there give me a headache. I miss the old feed store. It smelled like molasses and dust, and the guy who ran it, old Mr. Henderson, he had this three-legged dog that would just sleep on the porch all day. \n\nI think the dog's name was Buster. Or maybe Barnaby? Something with a B. He lost the leg getting hit by a tractor, they said. But he got around just fine. Dogs are resilient like that. They don't sit around feeling sorry for themselves, they just figure out how to walk on three legs and get on with it. \n\nBut anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the quiet hobbies. Well, I don't really know. I mean, I've heard the term before, mostly on the television or when people talk about kids in school. But for me? I'm not sure. It's just... the way I am, I guess. 

Speaking of television, they just don't make shows like they used to, do they? Everything now is all these reality programs with people yelling at each other on islands or in big houses. Or it's those crime shows where they solve a murder in forty-five minutes using some fancy computer that can zoom in on a reflection in a puddle from a satellite. Back in the day, you had proper stories. Like *Gunsmoke* or *The Andy Griffith Show*. 

Andy Griffith, now there was a show. Just a sheriff and his boy, and Barney Fife causing all sorts of trouble. Don Knotts was a genius, absolute genius. The way he could just shake and look nervous, it was pure comedy. My dad used to laugh so hard at Barney Fife that he'd start coughing and have to go get a glass of water. 

My dad drank a lot of water. Always had a big glass jar of it in the fridge with a slice of lemon in it. He said the lemon cut the dust from the factory. He worked at the old textile mill over in the next county. Spun cotton mostly, I think. The noise in that place was deafening. He had to wear these big heavy earmuffs all day, but he still lost most of his hearing by the time he was fifty. He used to say he didn't mind, though, because it meant he didn't have to listen to my mother's soap operas. 

She loved her stories, my mother. *Days of Our Lives*, *General Hospital*. She'd iron clothes in the living room just so she wouldn't miss a minute of it. The smell of hot iron on damp cotton... that always takes me right back to being a kid. 

But, uh... I lost the thread again, didn't I? You were asking about that ADHD thing. Yeah, I really don't know if that's what it is. I haven't really thought about it having a name like that.

He wears these fingerless gloves, the kind with the little mitten flap you can pull over. My grandmother used to knit those for us when we were kids. We called them glittens. She'd use this really itchy wool, though, so we hated wearing them. \n\nBut yeah, what was the question? Oh, distractions. Yeah, if I hear that truck or think about the garden, I completely lose where I was with my painting or my story. I'll look back at the paper and have no idea what I was trying to do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it difficult to focus or sit still in all situations, or are there certain places or activities where you can concentrate without much trouble?\n\nPatient: Well, I'd say it depends. If I'm out in the garden or tinkering with something, I'm okay. But if I have to sit through something quiet, like a long meeting or a church talk... oh boy. I just feel like I've got to shift around, tap my foot, or get up and stretch, even when I know I'm supposed to just sit there and listen. \n\nWe go to the First Presbyterian over on Elm Street. Beautiful old building, stained glass windows and everything. They replaced the pews a few years ago, though, and I swear they put in the hardest wood they could find. The old ones had these red velvet cushions that were starting to wear out—you could see the foam poking through on the end where Mrs. Higgins always sat. She's been going there since the fifties, I think. Always wears a hat. You don't see ladies wearing hats to church much anymore, do you? Just her. She makes a mean peach cobbler for the potlucks, though. She uses fresh peaches, never canned. Canned peaches always taste a little tinny to me, you know? Like you're eating the can itself. My wife buys them sometimes when they're on sale, but I just leave them in the pantry. \n\nBut anyway, yeah... sitting still in church or places like that. It's really hard. I just feel this urge to move my legs or shift my weight, and I can't seem to just stay put like everyone else.\n\nDoctor: Have you always been this way, or did you notice these difficulties with focusing and sitting still developing at some point in your life?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, it's pretty much been this way my whole life, near as I can tell. Even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling my parents I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils, calling out answers before they even called on me, and they constantly had to remind me to actually finish my work before I ran out for recess. \n\nRecess was the best part of the day, honestly. We used to play kickball out on this big asphalt lot behind the school. You had to be careful, though, because if you tripped on that asphalt, it would tear your knees right up. I remember Jimmy Peterson took a bad spill once, scraped himself up so bad his mom had to come get him. Jimmy’s mom drove this huge station wagon with the wood paneling on the side. You don't see cars like that anymore. Now everybody drives those little crossover SUVs that all look exactly the same. You walk out of the grocery store and you can't even tell which one is yours. My wife put a bright yellow antenna topper on ours—a little smiley face—just so we could find it in the lot at the Piggly Wiggly. \n\nBut anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, when it started. Yeah, it's always been there. Ever since I was a little kid, just losing things and having a hard time staying on track.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your difficulties with focusing and sitting still are affecting your overall well-being or daily life in a major way?\n\nPatient: Well, it's definitely a hassle, I guess you could say. It's gotten to the point where my wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me for just about everything. Which is a shame, because I used to try to keep my own pocket planner. I had this really nice leather one, dark brown, with my initials stamped in gold on the front. My daughter bought it for me for Father's Day a few years back. She got it at one of those little boutique shops downtown, the ones that sell artisanal soaps and candles that smell like pine needles and campfire smoke. I love that smell. Reminds me of when we used to take the kids camping up near the lake. We had this old canvas tent that weighed an absolute ton, and if it rained, you had to make sure you didn't touch the sides or the water would seep right through. \n\nWe used to cook hotdogs on sticks we found in the woods. You had to find the perfect stick, you know? Not too dry or it would catch fire, and it had to have a nice little fork at the end to hold the hotdog. Kids today, they have those metal extendable roasting forks you buy at the sporting goods store. Takes all the fun out of it, if you ask me. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, the calendar. I'd write things in that planner and then just forget to look at it, or I'd leave it on the workbench and lose it under a pile of sandpaper. So now she handles all that. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and the garden group more than once for letting people down—forgetting I was supposed to bring the mulch, or showing up on the wrong Tuesday for the planning committee. So, yeah, it definitely gets in the way of things.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble paying attention or that you act on impulse without thinking?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't really know if I could pick just one. I mean, they both seem to happen, don't they? Like, I'll be trying to pay attention to something, and then before I know it, I'm doing something else entirely without even thinking about it. Like last week, I was supposed to be fixing the hinge on the back gate. The screws had gotten all rusted out from all that rain we had in April. \n\nApril was just awful this year, wasn't it? Seemed like it rained every single day. My tomatoes didn't know what to do with themselves. They got that blossom end rot because the soil was just too damp for too long. You have to be careful with tomatoes, they like water but they don't like wet feet, as my grandfather used to say. He had this massive garden out behind his house. Grew everything. Corn, beans, squash. He used to make these little scarecrows out of old flannel shirts and pie tins to keep the crows away. The pie tins would clank together in the wind. It was a nice sound, actually. Very peaceful. \n\nBut anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the gate. Yeah, I went out to fix the gate, and I saw a weed in the flowerbed, so I pulled it. And then I saw another one, and the next thing I know, I've spent two hours pulling weeds and the gate is still broken. So I don't know if that's me not paying attention to the gate, or just impulsively pulling weeds. It all just sort of blends together for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your main problem is that you have trouble sitting still and being patient, or that you have trouble paying attention to details and following through on instructions?\n\nPatient: Well, it's funny you ask it that way, because I think it's a little bit of both, honestly, but maybe more the details part. Like, when I'm helping out with the volunteer storytelling flyers over at the community center, or even just jotting down my garden notes, I'm always messing something up. I'll miss putting the date on the flyer, or I'll leave out somebody's name entirely. Or out in the garden, I'll measure the fertilizer wrong, even though I swear I just looked right at the instructions. \n\nI used to use this liquid fertilizer that came in a bright green bottle. It smelled awful, like fish, but boy, did it make the hydrangeas bloom. My grandmother had hydrangeas all along the front of her porch. Huge blue ones. She said the trick was putting rusty nails in the soil to change the color. I don't know if that actually works or if it's just an old wives' tale, but she swore by it. She kept all her rusty nails in this old Folgers coffee can in the shed. You know the ones, the metal cans with the plastic lids? People used to keep everything in those. Screws, buttons, bacon grease... you name it. Now coffee comes in those bags that never seal right once you open them. I end up spilling coffee grounds all over the counter every single morning. My wife just sighs and hands me the sponge. She's a saint, really. \n\nBut anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, following through and details. Yeah, I'll think I looked a flyer over perfectly, or read the garden notes right, and then someone points out I completely missed a whole section. So I guess the attention to detail is definitely a big part of it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your ability to focus or sit still over the years, or has it remained relatively consistent?\n\nPatient: Well, I think it's been pretty much the exact same my whole life, to be honest. Even way back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils. \n\nSpeaking of pencils, remember those old metal sharpeners they used to have bolted right to the wall or the side of the teacher's desk? You had to crank them by hand. They made that loud grinding noise, and the smell of the cedar wood shavings... I always loved that smell. We used those yellow Ticonderoga pencils. If you bought the cheap ones, the lead would be broken all the way through the middle, and you'd sharpen it down to a tiny little nub and the lead would still just fall right out. My dad used to bring home these flat carpenter pencils from the job site. He was a framer, built houses all over the county. Those flat pencils wouldn't even fit in a normal sharpener, you had to whittle the end with a pocket knife. He had this old Case pocket knife with a bone handle that he kept razor sharp. He could peel an apple in one long, continuous strip with that thing. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, I'd lose my pencils constantly. And I was always getting in trouble for calling out answers in class without raising my hand. I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the teachers were always having to give me reminders to finish my work before I could go out for recess. \n\nRecess was the absolute best part of the day, though. We had this giant metal slide on the playground. By late spring, that metal would bake in the sun and get so hot it would practically blister the back of your legs if you were wearing shorts. But we didn't care one bit. We'd slide down it anyway, or we'd play tetherball until our knuckles were completely raw. Kids don't play tetherball much anymore, do they? Seems like a safety hazard nowadays, a heavy ball swinging around on a rope. \n\nSo, yeah... wait, what was it you just asked me? I think I lost the thread there. Oh, right, if it's changed over the years. No, I'd say it's been pretty consistent since I was a little boy.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD, or do you have any family members with the condition?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I've never been diagnosed with it or anything like that. Neither has anyone in my family, as far as I know. My brother, though, he was always bouncing off the walls, but back then they just called it having too much energy. He played football in high school. Linebacker. He was tough as nails, my brother. Broke his collarbone twice and just kept on playing. \n\nFootball was different back then, you know? The helmets didn't have all that padding they do now. They were practically just plastic shells with a little bit of foam inside. And the coaches, they wouldn't let you drink water during practice. Said it made you soft. Can you imagine that today? With all the heatstroke and everything, they'd be sued in a heartbeat. We used to sneak over to the hose behind the fieldhouse when the coach wasn't looking. That water tasted like rubber and rust, but it was the best thing I ever drank. \n\nMy brother actually got a scholarship to play at a small college up state, but he ended up blowing out his knee his freshman year. It was a shame, really. He loved the game. He ended up opening a hardware store instead. Sells everything from two-by-fours to those little tiny screws you need for eyeglasses. I was just in there last week looking for a specific kind of washer for the lawnmower. \n\nAnyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, diagnoses and family. No, no one's ever been officially diagnosed or treated for anything like that. Just the way we've always been, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you find so engaging or enjoyable that you can focus on them for long periods of time without getting distracted or feeling restless?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I try to find things like that. I really do. But I don't do well with quiet hobbies for very long anymore. Even when I'm just trying to sit and read a book or do a little sketching, I can't seem to just... do it. I'll start humming to myself, or talking out loud, or I'll just have to get up and mess with something in the room. \n\nI used to sketch a lot more when I was younger. Mostly birds. We had this big oak tree in the backyard, and the blue jays would just swarm the feeder. Blue jays are mean birds, though. They'll chase off all the cardinals and the finches just to get to the sunflower seeds. We used to buy the black oil sunflower seeds in these massive fifty-pound bags from the feed store down on Route 9. \n\nThat feed store is gone now, though. They tore it down to build one of those giant chain pharmacies. You know the ones, where they sell everything from milk to lawn chairs, but there's only ever one person working the register? The lines are always terrible. And the fluorescent lights in there give me a headache. I miss the old feed store. It smelled like molasses and dust, and the guy who ran it, old Mr. Henderson, he had this three-legged dog that would just sleep on the porch all day. \n\nI think the dog's name was Buster. Or maybe Barnaby? Something with a B. He lost the leg getting hit by a tractor, they said. But he got around just fine. Dogs are resilient like that. They don't sit around feeling sorry for themselves, they just figure out how to walk on three legs and get on with it. \n\nBut anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the quiet hobbies. Yeah, reading or sketching, I just end up fidgeting or getting up to fiddle with the blinds or something. I just can't stay settled with it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties are more related to not being able to pay attention to details or to being overly active and restless?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, but the details really do trip me up quite a bit. Like, when I help out with the volunteer storytelling flyers down at the center, or when I'm writing down my garden notes, I’ll just completely miss a date, or I'll leave out somebody's name. Or I'll measure something wrong out in the yard, even though I could have sworn I looked it over real careful. \n\nSpeaking of the yard, I was measuring for some new tomato stakes recently. I grow those big heirloom tomatoes, the Brandywines. They get so heavy you have to tie them up to the stakes with strips of old pantyhose so the stems don't snap. My grandmother taught me that trick. She had a garden the size of a baseball diamond out behind her place. Grew absolutely everything under the sun. Corn, squash, pole beans. She used to can her own green beans in those heavy glass mason jars. You'd sit in the kitchen and just wait to hear that sharp little \"pop\" sound when the lids sealed as they cooled down on the counter. \n\nWe kept all those jars down in the root cellar. That cellar always smelled like damp earth and old potatoes. There was an old iron coal chute down there, too, from back before they put the oil furnace in. The coal truck would pull right up to the side of the house and just rattle all that coal right down the chute. It made a terrible racket, and the coal dust would get on absolutely everything. You'd be wiping black soot off the windowsills for a week after a delivery. \n\nWait, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Losing the track. What was it you were asking me about? Oh, right, the details or being restless. Yeah, it's the details that get me. Just missing dates on those flyers and messing up my garden measurements, mostly, no matter how hard I try to double-check things.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with focusing and sitting still might be related to ADHD?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't really know. I mean, I've heard the term before, mostly on the television or when people talk about kids in school. But for me? I'm not sure. It's just... the way I am, I guess. \n\nSpeaking of television, they just don't make shows like they used to, do they? Everything now is all these reality programs with people yelling at each other on islands or in big houses. Or it's those crime shows where they solve a murder in forty-five minutes using some fancy computer that can zoom in on a reflection in a puddle from a satellite. Back in the day, you had proper stories. Like *Gunsmoke* or *The Andy Griffith Show*. \n\nAndy Griffith, now there was a show. Just a sheriff and his boy, and Barney Fife causing all sorts of trouble. Don Knotts was a genius, absolute genius. The way he could just shake and look nervous, it was pure comedy. My dad used to laugh so hard at Barney Fife that he'd start coughing and have to go get a glass of water. \n\nMy dad drank a lot of water. Always had a big glass jar of it in the fridge with a slice of lemon in it. He said the lemon cut the dust from the factory. He worked at the old textile mill over in the next county. Spun cotton mostly, I think. The noise in that place was deafening. He had to wear these big heavy earmuffs all day, but he still lost most of his hearing by the time he was fifty. He used to say he didn't mind, though, because it meant he didn't have to listen to my mother's soap operas. \n\nShe loved her stories, my mother. *Days of Our Lives*, *General Hospital*. She'd iron clothes in the living room just so she wouldn't miss a minute of it. The smell of hot iron on damp cotton... that always takes me right back to being a kid. \n\nBut, uh... I lost the thread again, didn't I? You were asking about that ADHD thing. Yeah, I really don't know if that's what it is. I haven't really thought about it having a name like that.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. She said the trick was putting rusty nails in the soil to change the color. I don't know if that actually works or if it's just an old wives' tale, but she swore by it. She kept all her rusty nails in this old Folgers coffee can in the shed. You know the ones, the metal cans with the plastic lids? People used to keep everything in those. Screws, buttons, bacon grease... you name it. Now coffee comes in those bags that never seal right once you open them. I end up spilling coffee grounds all over the counter every single morning. My wife just sighs and hands me the sponge. She's a saint, really. \n\nBut anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, following through and details. Yeah, I'll think I looked a flyer over perfectly, or read the garden notes right, and then someone points out I completely missed a whole section. So I guess the attention to detail is definitely a big part of it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your ability to focus or sit still over the years, or has it remained relatively consistent?\n\nPatient: Well, I think it's been pretty much the exact same my whole life, to be honest. Even way back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was bright but just scattered. I was always losing my pencils. \n\nSpeaking of pencils, remember those old metal sharpeners they used to have bolted right to the wall or the side of the teacher's desk? You had to crank them by hand. They made that loud grinding noise, and the smell of the cedar wood shavings... I always loved that smell. We used those yellow Ticonderoga pencils. If you bought the cheap ones, the lead would be broken all the way through the middle, and you'd sharpen it down to a tiny little nub and the lead would still just fall right out. My dad used to bring home these flat carpenter pencils from the job site. He was a framer, built houses all over the county. Those flat pencils wouldn't even fit in a normal sharpener, you had to whittle the end with a pocket knife. He had this old Case pocket knife with a bone handle that he kept razor sharp. He could peel an apple in one long, continuous strip with that thing. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, I'd lose my pencils constantly. And I was always getting in trouble for calling out answers in class without raising my hand. I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the teachers were always having to give me reminders to finish my work before I could go out for recess. \n\nRecess was the absolute best part of the day, though. We had this giant metal slide on the playground. By late spring, that metal would bake in the sun and get so hot it would practically blister the back of your legs if you were wearing shorts. But we didn't care one bit. We'd slide down it anyway, or we'd play tetherball until our knuckles were completely raw. Kids don't play tetherball much anymore, do they? Seems like a safety hazard nowadays, a heavy ball swinging around on a rope. \n\nSo, yeah... wait, what was it you just asked me? I think I lost the thread there. Oh, right, if it's changed over the years. No, I'd say it's been pretty consistent since I was a little boy.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for ADHD, or do you have any family members with the condition?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I've never been diagnosed with it or anything like that. Neither has anyone in my family, as far as I know. My brother, though, he was always bouncing off the walls, but back then they just called it having too much energy. He played football in high school. Linebacker. He was tough as nails, my brother. Broke his collarbone twice and just kept on playing. \n\nFootball was different back then, you know? The helmets didn't have all that padding they do now. They were practically just plastic shells with a little bit of foam inside. And the coaches, they wouldn't let you drink water during practice. Said it made you soft. Can you imagine that today? With all the heatstroke and everything, they'd be sued in a heartbeat. We used to sneak over to the hose behind the fieldhouse when the coach wasn't looking. That water tasted like rubber and rust, but it was the best thing I ever drank. \n\nMy brother actually got a scholarship to play at a small college up state, but he ended up blowing out his knee his freshman year. It was a shame, really. He loved the game. He ended up opening a hardware store instead. Sells everything from two-by-fours to those little tiny screws you need for eyeglasses. I was just in there last week looking for a specific kind of washer for the lawnmower. \n\nAnyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, diagnoses and family. No, no one's ever been officially diagnosed or treated for anything like that. Just the way we've always been, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you find so engaging or enjoyable that you can focus on them for long periods of time without getting distracted or feeling restless?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, I try to find things like that. I really do. But I don't do well with quiet hobbies for very long anymore. Even when I'm just trying to sit and read a book or do a little sketching, I can't seem to just... do it. I'll start humming to myself, or talking out loud, or I'll just have to get up and mess with something in the room. \n\nI used to sketch a lot more when I was younger. Mostly birds. We had this big oak tree in the backyard, and the blue jays would just swarm the feeder. Blue jays are mean birds, though. They'll chase off all the cardinals and the finches just to get to the sunflower seeds. We used to buy the black oil sunflower seeds in these massive fifty-pound bags from the feed store down on Route 9. \n\nThat feed store is gone now, though. They tore it down to build one of those giant chain pharmacies. You know the ones, where they sell everything from milk to lawn chairs, but there's only ever one person working the register? The lines are always terrible. And the fluorescent lights in there give me a headache. I miss the old feed store. It smelled like molasses and dust, and the guy who ran it, old Mr. Henderson, he had this three-legged dog that would just sleep on the porch all day. \n\nI think the dog's name was Buster. Or maybe Barnaby? Something with a B. He lost the leg getting hit by a tractor, they said. But he got around just fine. Dogs are resilient like that. They don't sit around feeling sorry for themselves, they just figure out how to walk on three legs and get on with it. \n\nBut anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the quiet hobbies. Yeah, reading or sketching, I just end up fidgeting or getting up to fiddle with the blinds or something. I just can't stay settled with it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties are more related to not being able to pay attention to details or to being overly active and restless?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, but the details really do trip me up quite a bit. Like, when I help out with the volunteer storytelling flyers down at the center, or when I'm writing down my garden notes, I’ll just completely miss a date, or I'll leave out somebody's name. Or I'll measure something wrong out in the yard, even though I could have sworn I looked it over real careful. \n\nSpeaking of the yard, I was measuring for some new tomato stakes recently. I grow those big heirloom tomatoes, the Brandywines. They get so heavy you have to tie them up to the stakes with strips of old pantyhose so the stems don't snap. My grandmother taught me that trick. She had a garden the size of a baseball diamond out behind her place. Grew absolutely everything under the sun. Corn, squash, pole beans. She used to can her own green beans in those heavy glass mason jars. You'd sit in the kitchen and just wait to hear that sharp little \"pop\" sound when the lids sealed as they cooled down on the counter. \n\nWe kept all those jars down in the root cellar. That cellar always smelled like damp earth and old potatoes. There was an old iron coal chute down there, too, from back before they put the oil furnace in. The coal truck would pull right up to the side of the house and just rattle all that coal right down the chute. It made a terrible racket, and the coal dust would get on absolutely everything. You'd be wiping black soot off the windowsills for a week after a delivery. \n\nWait, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Losing the track. What was it you were asking me about? Oh, right, the details or being restless. Yeah, it's the details that get me. Just missing dates on those flyers and messing up my garden measurements, mostly, no matter how hard I try to double-check things.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with focusing and sitting still might be related to ADHD?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't really know. I mean, I've heard the term before, mostly on the television or when people talk about kids in school. But for me? I'm not sure. It's just... the way I am, I guess. \n\nSpeaking of television, they just don't make shows like they used to, do they? Everything now is all these reality programs with people yelling at each other on islands or in big houses. Or it's those crime shows where they solve a murder in forty-five minutes using some fancy computer that can zoom in on a reflection in a puddle from a satellite. Back in the day, you had proper stories. Like *Gunsmoke* or *The Andy Griffith Show*. \n\nAndy Griffith, now there was a show. Just a sheriff and his boy, and Barney Fife causing all sorts of trouble. Don Knotts was a genius, absolute genius. The way he could just shake and look nervous, it was pure comedy. My dad used to laugh so hard at Barney Fife that he'd start coughing and have to go get a glass of water. \n\nMy dad drank a lot of water. Always had a big glass jar of it in the fridge with a slice of lemon in it. He said the lemon cut the dust from the factory. He worked at the old textile mill over in the next county. Spun cotton mostly, I think. The noise in that place was deafening. He had to wear these big heavy earmuffs all day, but he still lost most of his hearing by the time he was fifty. He used to say he didn't mind, though, because it meant he didn't have to listen to my mother's soap operas. \n\nShe loved her stories, my mother. *Days of Our Lives*, *General Hospital*. She'd iron clothes in the living room just so she wouldn't miss a minute of it. The smell of hot iron on damp cotton... that always takes me right back to being a kid. \n\nBut, uh... I lost the thread again, didn't I? You were asking about that ADHD thing. Yeah, I really don't know if that's what it is. I haven't really thought about it having a name like that.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your main difficulty is with staying focused on tasks or with feeling restless and fidgety?\n\nPatient: Well, I'd say the restlessness is a pretty big one for me. Like, if I'm sitting through a quiet meeting or a church talk, I just feel like I’ve got to shift around in my seat, or I'll start tapping my foot. I just get this overwhelming urge to get up and stretch, even when I know I really should just stay put and be polite. \n\nSpeaking of church, our pastor, Reverend Davis, he can really stretch a sermon out. Nice man, though. His wife plays the organ. It's one of those beautiful old pipe organs, you know the kind? With all the wooden pedals and the big brass pipes up on the wall. They had to get a specialist all the way from Chicago just to come tune the thing last spring. Cost the congregation a small fortune. We had to do a whole month of bake sales just to cover the travel expenses for the tuning fella. \n\nI made three cherry pies for that sale. Used my mother's old recipe. The secret is a little bit of almond extract in the filling, it really makes the cherries pop. And you have to use real lard in the crust. People are so scared of lard these days, but it's what makes the pastry actually flake. You cut it in ice-cold with a pastry blender, and you have to use ice water, too, or the fat melts before it even hits the oven... \n\nWait, goodness, I'm doing it again. I'm sorry, I get to talking about baking and I just lose the whole point of the conversation. You were asking about the fidgeting. But yes, it's definitely the restlessness. Sitting in those pews or anywhere quiet, I just can't keep my feet still to save my life."
